title: Orion BioSystems - Privacy Ops & Trust Boundary Review
summary: Customer requested deep dive on data handling: explicit confirmation that customer content is not used to train models, prompt retention windows, PII/PHI handling, KMS/HSM key flow, SOC2/ISO artifacts, RBAC and SSO integration options, and EU data residency. Agreed next steps: share SOC 2 report, architecture diagram for private deployment, and sample audit log extract; schedule short follow-up demo of Private deployment networking (VPC peering) and key management. Redwood has a formal "no-training-on-customer-data" policy for hosted and dedicated customers.
topics: Encryption at-rest and in-transit, KMS/HSM flow
Data residency (EU) and Private deployment options
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-22 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: available
Attendees: Nina Patel (Redwood AE), Marcus Li (Redwood SE), Dr. Elena Ruiz (Orion), Samir Kapoor (Orion), Joanne Miller (Orion legal), Ben Carter (Orion infra)

Summary (auto): quick security walkthrough, confirm no training on customer data, review KMS flow and how prompt data is handled, next steps to share SOC2 and architecture.

00:00:05 Nina Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Um this is Nina from Redwood, and with me is Marcus, our solutions engineer. Um who's on from Orion?
00:00:15 Dr. Elena Ruiz: Hi, Elena here. I'm Head of Privacy at Orion. We also have Samir, Joanne, Ben on the call. Thanks for doing this.
00:00:25 Nina Patel: Great, thanks. The plan for today is to walk through our data handling commitments — especially the bit about not training models on customer content — and then Marcus will go into the KMS and audit logs. We'll leave time for Q&A. Sound good?
00:00:37 Samir Kapoor: Yep, that's perfect.
00:01:00 Marcus Li: Okay, I'll start with a quick architecture sketch. So at a high level in our hosted mode, requests come into the API gateway, TLS in transit, token validated at the edge, routed to inference pools. We do prefix caching and KV cache, uh that's our internal term, and then KV cache is ephemeral per request.
00:01:25 Ben Carter: Sorry, Marcus — can you repeat KV cache? The recording transcribed it as K V cash in our notes earlier and we wanna be sure.
00:01:30 Marcus Li: Yeah sorry, KV cache — key-value cache. It's ephemeral, not persisted beyond the request unless you enable explicit caching.
00:01:43 Dr. Elena Ruiz: Can you confirm: does any of our prompt or completions get used to fine-tune or update the base models? We have strict rules prohibiting training on customer data.
00:01:55 Nina Patel: Short answer: no. Redwood has a formal "no-training-on-customer-data" policy for hosted and dedicated customers. We do not feed customer prompts or their completions back into model training pipelines. I'll read the exact wording after Marcus explains how we separate telemetry from content.
00:02:12 Marcus Li: Right, and to add to that, we collect telemetry for service health — e.g., latency histograms, error rates, token counts — which are aggregated. The raw prompt text is not stored long-term unless retention is enabled by the customer. For customers that require zero retention we offer Private deployments where the control plane can be customer-managed.
00:02:36 Joanne Miller: How do you prove that in audits? SOC 2 wants to see data handling controls and evidence.
00:02:45 Nina Patel: We can provide our SOC 2 Type II report plus a disclosure statement. We also provide a data flow diagram and a sample audit logs extract that shows redaction of PII. I'll attach those after the call.
00:02:58 Samir Kapoor: On the encryption side — KMS, HSM — how are keys managed for hosted customers? Do you hold keys or do we bring our own?
00:03:10 Marcus Li: Two options: hosted default uses Redwood-managed KMS with customer-specific keys isolated per account. We encrypt at rest using AES-256 and TLS 1.3 in transit. For customers who need full control we support BYOK via customer KMS and HSM integration — that's supported for Dedicated and Private deployments. In BYOK mode, the key material never leaves your KMS/HSM.
00:03:36 Ben Carter: If we do BYOK, do you store any cache or logs that could include prompt snippets? We need to ensure logs are redacted.
00:03:45 Marcus Li: Audit logs can be configured to redact prompt content. By default we log metadata (request id, model used, latency, token counts) and hashes for content if needed for dedup. If you need zero content in logs we can set to redact the content field and store only the hash. Example log snippet we'll share shows "content: [REDACTED]" and an optional content_sha256 field.
00:04:10 Dr. Elena Ruiz: What's your default retention for prompts and completions in hosted mode?
00:04:18 Nina Patel: Default is 30 days for debug/debugging artifacts, 90 days for rolling analytics aggregates, but actual raw text prompts are kept for 7 days by default. However, customers can opt into shorter windows or opt out entirely. We also have an explicit setting in the Console: "prompt retention policy".
00:04:36 Dr. Elena Ruiz: Seven days is too long for us for anything containing PHI. We need either ephemeral storage or tokenization/pseudonymization before it reaches Redwood.
00:04:46 Marcus Li: Understood. For PHI we recommend 2 approaches: 1) Push to Private deployment inside your VPC so data never crosses our hosted plane; or 2) implement client-side pseudonymization — we have a lightweight SDK that can pseudonymize obvious identifiers before sending. We can also run a pre-processing step (redaction using regex/NER) in your network.
00:05:10 Joanne Miller: If we go Private, what does the compliance evidence look like? We still need Redwood's SOC 2 statements because the software is Redwood's.
00:05:20 Nina Patel: Correct, Private customers still get Redwood's SOC 2 Type II coverage on the software and controls that Redwood operates. The difference is the data plane can be customer-hosted; we provide the control plane options and the deployment manifest. We'll provide an SOC 2 bridge letter and a deployment diagram.
00:05:36 Samir Kapoor: On RBAC/SSO — can we provision roles from our identity provider? We use Okta and SCIM.
00:05:45 Marcus Li: Yes, we support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC is role-based and you can map Okta groups to Redwood roles. We also have fine-grained route-level permissions if you need to restrict who can call generation endpoints vs who can view billing or audit logs.
00:06:05 Ben Carter: Are there logs for who accessed what prompt? We need for e-discovery.
00:06:12 Marcus Li: Yes audit logs include user identity, IP, action (e.g., /v1/generate), request id, timestamp. Content can be redacted but the metadata remains for audit. Retention policy for logs is configurable — default 90 days, extendable to 7 years for enterprise plans — we can ship logs to your SIEM (Splunk/Sumo/Elastic) via streaming.
00:06:35 Dr. Elena Ruiz: Important to ensure that logs stored in third-party SIEMs are encrypted under our keys.
00:06:42 Marcus Li: We support log streaming over secure pipes; for hosted logs we can encrypt with customer-managed keys, and for Private logs you control the storage entirely.
00:06:52 Joanne Miller: Quick question on data residency: we need EU-only processing for certain datasets. How does Redwood handle region pinning?
00:07:03 Nina Patel: We have region pinning for both Hosted and Dedicated. For Hosted we can pin requests to EU regions; for Dedicated and Private you can deploy entirely in an EU region or on-prem. We'll share the region catalog and the SLA differences.
00:07:18 Samir Kapoor: On the "no training on customer data" — is that a legal contract clause? We want it in the agreement and need to know exceptions, if any.
00:07:28 Nina Patel: Yes, we can include a contractual clause: "Redwood will not use Customer data to train models nor to improve model weights". The common exception is aggregate telemetry for service quality that does not include raw customer content; we'll put language around aggregation and redaction. We'll work with Joanne to add the clause.
00:07:45 Joanne Miller: We'll want defined meanings for 'customer data' and 'aggregate telemetry' in the contract. Also, if Redwood ever wants to run a cross-customer eval we need an opt-in flow and a legal attestation that data used is non-customer or explicitly consented.
00:08:00 Nina Patel: That matches our standard practice. Marcus, do you want to show the audit log sample?
00:08:05 Marcus Li: Sure, I'm pasting a sample in the chat: {timestamp, request_id, user: "joanne@orion.com", endpoint: "/v1/generate", content: "[REDACTED]", content_sha256: "a1b2c3...", model: "rwd-base-3b", latency_ms: 210}. Note the content_sha256 is optional and only stored if the customer enables content hashing for dedup / caching purposes.
00:08:35 Ben Carter: That content_sha— is that reversible? If someone gets the hash can they recover text?
00:08:40 Marcus Li: It's a SHA-256 hash; not reversible. If you need salted hashing we support HMAC with a customer key.
00:08:48 Dr. Elena Ruiz: For PHI we need to ensure that the pre-processing/redaction is auditable. Can Redwood provide a cert or an algorithm description of the redaction method?
00:08:59 Marcus Li: We have an internal NER-based redaction preprocessor we can describe in a tech note. For regulatory audits we can provide algorithm docs and test vectors under NDA.
00:09:12 Samir Kapoor: Can you explain the difference between Dedicated and Private for our use case?
00:09:20 Nina Patel: Short: Dedicated = Redwood-managed infra reserved for you, isolated tenancy, Redwood still manages the control plane; Private = you host the data plane or have a VPC with customer-managed networking and optionally on-prem. For the strictest controls (PHI inside EU, BYOK, egress controls) Private is the recommended path.
00:09:40 Joanne Miller: What's the timeline for a Private pilot? We need to show feasibility within Q2.
00:09:46 Nina Patel: We typically spin up a Private pilot in 2-4 weeks depending on networking approvals. Action: we'll scope the pilot with infra requirements.
00:09:55 Samir Kapoor: Are there known performance or feature tradeoffs on Private?
00:10:00 Marcus Li: Mostly around autoscaling and novel kernels — on some custom hardware we may need to tune the runtime. We provide the same feature set, but for bleeding-edge kernel optimizations we might require a short tuning window. For standard open models performance parity is close.
00:10:20 Dr. Elena Ruiz: Another concern: regulatory requests — e.g., subpoenas — how do you handle data requests? Who gets notified?
00:10:30 Nina Patel: We have a legal intake process. For Hosted accounts we notify the customer and follow the contract's terms unless prohibited. For Private deployments we send the legal request to the point-of-contact and coordinate. We'll supply a transparency report sample.
00:10:45 Joanne Miller: Great. Can you share an example clause for notification timelines? We want 48 hours notice unless prohibited.
00:10:52 Nina Patel: We can propose a 48-72 hour notification clause; I'll follow up with suggested language.
00:11:05 Marcus Li: Quick note on SSO provisioning: SCIM sync can provision groups nightly or near-real-time; we recommend role gating for production APIs and separate keys for non-prod.
00:11:20 Ben Carter: Do you support hardware attestations for the runtime? Like IMA/TPM attestation?
00:11:27 Marcus Li: For Private we can bring attestations depending on the on-prem infra. For Dedicated we can provide host attestations on request; some customers require FIPS/HSM-backed endpoints which we support in certain regions.
00:11:45 Dr. Elena Ruiz: Last question — are prompts ever used for model evals (not training) across customers? For example, sampling anonymized prompts to test regressions.
00:11:56 Nina Patel: Only with explicit consent. We have an opt-in flag and legal attestation; and we require that any sampled prompts are anonymized/pseudonymized. By default we do not do cross-customer evals using raw prompts.
00:12:10 Samir Kapoor: Okay thanks. I think that's most of our questions.
00:12:15 Nina Patel: Great. Quick recap and next steps: we'll send SOC 2 Type II, an architecture diagram for Private, sample redacted audit log, and contract language for the no-training clause. We'll also propose dates for a Private pilot kickoff.
00:12:30 Dr. Elena Ruiz: Good. Can we also get a short checklist for onboard — e.g., SCIM group names, network CIDR requirements, KMS endpoints?
00:12:40 Nina Patel: Yep we'll include an onboarding checklist. Marcus, anything to add?
00:12:45 Marcus Li: I'll add the KMS flow diagram and sample log extract, and prep a short demo for Private networking (VPC peering) — propose next week for that 30-minute session.
00:12:58 Joanne Miller: Thanks, sounds good.
00:13:05 Nina Patel: Thank you all. We'll follow up with docs in 48 hours.
00:13:12 (meeting closes)
